newsitem.title: UK: Tesco outlook boosts UK supermarkets. [CORRECTED 17:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Tesco outlook boosts UK supermarkets. [CORRECTED 17:30 GMT]

text.p: Leading British supermarket group Tesco Plc reported a 10 percent rise in profits, as expected, on Tuesday and enlivened the food retail sector with prospects for more stable margins.
"The market liked the suggestion that gross margins could stabilise this year ... the background looks more favourable," said Dave Stoddart of brokers Henderson Crosthwaite.

Tesco turned in pretax profits of 750 million pounds ($1.2 billion), up from 675 million previously, and in line with market expectations. It paid out a total dividend of 10.35 pence, compared with 9.6 last year.
The company said that sales based on the same number of stores were up six percent in the first four weeks of the current year.
"This is a good start in a competitive environment," Lord MacLaurin, who retires as chairman later this year, said.
Tesco shares were up 12-1/2 pence to 365 pence by 1450 GMT, while rival ASDA had gained four to 111-1/2 in strong volumes and Safeway added 6-1/2 to 371.
But arch-rival J. Sainsbury slipped seven pence to 326. Traders attributed this to technical factors involving one large trade.
Tesco said that operating margins (corrects from "gross margins") slipped 0.4 percent to 5.8 percent last year but 0.3 point of the slide was due to a fierce petrol price war in the first half.

Deputy chairman David Reid told Reuters: "We are anticipating next year to be a stabilising picture on margins ... petrol margins are recovering and there seems to be some reasonable stability in food prices currently."
He said food price inflation was currently around zero and added that "we think low inflation will probably stay on through until about the autumn."
"It looks more benign on the margin front and relatively flat industry gross margins are good for the sector as a whole," said one industry analyst.
"The underlying conditions for the superstore sector are favourable (and) should allow all leading superstore groups to find growth," MacLaurin told a news conference.
Reid said that for Tesco, maintaining gross margins would be the key during the current year.
"I think it will still be very competitive. I think the noise level will still be high ... I think you can see that just from the various promotions that are going on."

But MacLaurin said there was little prospect of a price war because of low inflation and the very competitive environment as supermarkets focused on wooing customers with service and their range of products.
Tesco aims to launch a credit card in early July as a first step in its financial services venture with Royal Bank of Scotland, with other products to follow, Reid said.
The superstore chain, which has a market share of 14.5 percent, compared with Sainsbury's 12 percent in second place, considers its product offers to customers to be the key, MacLaurin said.
Analysts said Tesco's plans on new store openings and extensions also boosted sentiment as they appeared to be more in line with predicted demand.
"Space opening versus demand is a better mix than it has been for some time," Stoddart said.
Tesco aims to open 26 stores in Britain this year totalling around 600,000 sq feet (55,700 sq metres), along with about 200,000 sq feet (18,500 sq metres) of extensions.
Reid said the management transition as MacLaurin steps down, leaving Terry Leahy as chief executive, was proceeding smoothly and the new team would provide "more of the same".

He said that would include more customer initiatives based on "better prices, improved service, working very hard with ClubCard...further new products and particularly also more money going into refits and extensions."

The company expected its recent purchase of Irish supermarkets from Associated British Foods (ABF) for 630 million pounds to see a return on capital on a depreciation basis of around 15 percent, compared with around nine percent on the acquisition cost.
